paragraphs.source_en: When examining the Bubaline engravings in the Messak, Cremaschi (1992) noticed that under the patina there are marked traces of erosion that occurred before the patina formed. The degree of erosion suggests that it can have occurred in two different circumstances; either during the hyperarid period of the Late Pleistocene, caused by strong aeolian erosion, or during very wet climatic conditions caused by running water which eroded the engravings before the patina formed. It cannot therefore be excluded that the engravings were created during the last millennia of the Pleistocene (Lupacciolu 1978; Hachid 1998; Aumassip 2004). At Tin Ascigh in the Acacus, Mori (1974) found three superimposed engraved animals, each with a different colour of patina. The lowest engraving of a Bubalus antiquus with a black patina is superimposed by a giraffe with a lighter patina.

paragraphs.source_en: The uppermost engraving is of another giraffe with the lightest patina. According to Mori the difference between the patina of the three engravings is so marked that several millennia separate their creation. Based on field research in the Acacus, on indirect 14C dating and on superimpositions, Mori thus proposes that the earliest engravings belong to the Bubaline style at or before 10,000 BP, and the later engravings belong to the Pastoral phase starting at 7,500 BP (Mori 1974; 2000).

paragraphs.source_en: A very different opinion about the Bubaline style and dating is expressed by the main supporter of the low chronology Muzzolini (1995a, b; 1996). He refutes the traditional statement that the Bubaline style depicts only wild fauna and he points out that a large number of clearly domesticated cattle and sheep are represented in the same style, technique and patina as the Bubaline wild animals. These engravings are inextricably mixed with the wild fauna on the same walls or in the same sites. For this reason, he places all engravings into one single group called Bubaline but chronologically dated after 7,000 BP, which corresponds to the beginnings of the domestication attested in the Sahara.
